# The Hidden Geometry of Proofs

## When mathematicians discovered that proofs have shapes, distances, and landscapes

---

Imagine you're trying to compress a proof — not the kind you write on a blackboard, but the sprawling logical argument a computer uses to verify that a bridge will hold or that a cryptographic protocol is secure. These proofs can be enormous: millions of logical steps, each depending on the last. How do you know when two proofs are "really the same"? How do you compress one without losing its essential content?

For decades, mathematicians and computer scientists treated proofs as purely syntactic objects — sequences of symbols following rigid rules. You could measure their length, count their steps, time how long they take to verify. But something was missing. There was no way to talk about the *shape* of a proof, the *distance* between two proofs, or the *geometry* of the space where all possible proofs live.

Until now.

## The Observer Lens

The breakthrough begins with a simple but powerful idea: instead of looking at proofs directly, look at them through **observers**. An observer is like a lens that blurs certain details while preserving others. Mathematically, it's a "congruence relation" — a way of declaring that certain proof states are equivalent from a particular viewpoint.

Think of it this way. You have a complex proof, and you hand it to three different experts. The first expert cares only about whether the proof uses induction. The second cares only about whether it references prime numbers. The third tracks whether it invokes the axiom of choice. Each expert gives you a simplified verdict: from their perspective, your proof is one of a few possible types.

No single expert sees the whole picture. But together, they might. If every pair of distinct proofs is told apart by at least one expert, then the collection of expert verdicts — the **observer family** — captures everything that matters about the proof system.

This is the algebraic starting point: proofs live in a semiring (a structure with addition and multiplication, like the natural numbers), and observers are congruences that partition the semiring into equivalence classes.

## From Algebra to Geography

Here is where the geometry enters. Each observer defines a "point" in a new space — the **prime congruence spectrum** of the proof semiring. Just as geographers chart the Earth by triangulating from survey points, mathematicians can chart proof systems by plotting their observers.

The spectrum is not just a set of points. It comes with a natural **topology** — a notion of which sets are "open" — inherited from the algebraic structure. The basic open sets are defined by *separation*: given two proof elements a and b, the set D(a,b) consists of all observers that can tell a from b. These separation sets generate the entire topology, much like the open intervals generate the topology of the real number line.

The first major result: this spectral topology satisfies the **T₀ separation axiom**. In plain language, if two observers are topologically indistinguishable — they belong to exactly the same open sets — then they are actually the same observer. The geometry has enough resolution to see every distinct viewpoint.

## A Non-Archimedean Distance

But topology alone is just qualitative. The real surprise is that the spectrum carries a natural **ultrametric** — a distance function that is even stronger than the usual triangle inequality.

In ordinary geometry, the triangle inequality says the direct path between two points is never longer than any detour: d(A,C) ≤ d(A,B) + d(B,C). An ultrametric replaces the sum with a maximum: d(A,C) ≤ max(d(A,B), d(B,C)). This sounds like a minor tweak, but it changes everything. In an ultrametric space, every triangle is isosceles. Every ball is simultaneously open and closed. The space fragments into a tree-like hierarchy of clusters within clusters.

The ultrametric on the proof spectrum comes from **agreement depth**. Given a sequence of test pairs — fingerprints that probe different aspects of the proof structure — two observers are "close" if they agree on the first many tests and "far" if they disagree early. The distance is (1/2) raised to the power of the first disagreement index. Observers that agree on everything are distance zero; observers that disagree immediately are distance one.

This is exactly how p-adic numbers work. In the p-adic world, two numbers are "close" if their difference is divisible by a high power of a prime p. The proof spectrum inherits this same non-Archimedean flavor: proximity means agreement on deeper and deeper levels of structure, like two trees that share a longer and longer common trunk before their branches diverge.

## The Reconstruction Theorem

The crown jewel is the **reconstruction theorem**: the spectral evaluation map is injective.

What does this mean? Given any element a of the proof semiring, you can evaluate it at every observer to get a function on the spectrum — a "spectral profile." The reconstruction theorem says that if two elements have the same spectral profile (every observer treats them identically), then they are equivalent in the combined kernel of all observers.

In other words: the proof is completely determined by how it looks to its observers. The abstract algebraic object (the proof) can be faithfully reconstructed from the geometric object (its profile on the spectrum). This is the proof-semiring analogue of classical Stone duality, which says that a Boolean algebra is completely determined by its space of prime filters.

The evaluation map does more than separate elements. It is a **ring homomorphism** into a product of quotient semirings — it preserves the algebraic operations of the proof system. Addition and multiplication of proofs correspond to pointwise operations on their spectral profiles.

## A Contravariant Functor

The final piece of the architecture is **functoriality**. A morphism between proof semirings — a ring homomorphism φ: S → T — induces a map in the *opposite* direction on spectra: Spec(T) → Spec(S). This "pullback" takes an observer on T and pulls it back to an observer on S by precomposing with φ.

This reversal of arrows is the hallmark of duality. In algebraic geometry, a map of rings gives a map of spaces in the opposite direction. In our setting, a proof compression map S → T (which simplifies proofs) becomes, geometrically, an expansion of the observer space. Compression in the algebraic world is expansion in the geometric world. Every simplification opens new viewpoints.

The pullback map is continuous (it preserves the topological structure) and nonexpansive (it never increases distances). This means that proof transformations are geometrically well-behaved: they can shrink the landscape but never stretch it.

## Why It Matters

Why should anyone care that proofs have an ultrametric geometry?

**For computer science**: Proof compression is a bottleneck in formal verification. The spectral perspective suggests new compression strategies: instead of working syntactically (shortening the proof text), work geometrically (projecting onto lower-dimensional observer spaces). The ultrametric structure means that small perturbations in observer choice lead to small changes in the compressed representation — a stability guarantee that syntactic methods lack.

**For cryptography**: The diagonal avoidance condition — every distinct pair is separated by some observer — is exactly the collision resistance property needed for hash families. The spectral framework gives a unified algebraic foundation for designing and analyzing hash functions, with the observer count providing explicit security parameter bounds.

**For mathematics**: The construction opens a new field of "non-Archimedean proof geometry." Just as algebraic geometry studies solution sets of polynomial equations through their spectra, this framework studies proof systems through their observer spectra. The tools of p-adic analysis, tropical geometry, and Stone duality become available for analyzing proofs.

**For machine learning**: Observers are features. The spectrum is a latent space. The reconstruction theorem says this latent space is complete — no information is lost. This provides a mathematical foundation for "proof representation learning," where neural networks learn to embed proofs in geometric spaces for downstream tasks like proof search and theorem suggestion.

## The Bigger Picture

In 1936, Marshall Stone proved that every Boolean algebra is isomorphic to the algebra of clopen sets of a compact totally disconnected space. This was one of the first great dualities in mathematics, bridging abstract logic and concrete geometry.

The proof semiring spectrum extends this vision to a richer algebraic setting — semirings instead of Boolean algebras — and a richer geometric setting — ultrametric spaces instead of merely topological ones. The passage from Boolean to semiring captures the quantitative, compositional structure of proofs. The passage from topology to ultrametric captures their hierarchical, tree-like nature.

What makes this particularly striking is the role of self-reference. Proofs can refer to themselves — they can encode their own structure, diagonalize, and generate paradoxes. The diagonal avoidance condition is precisely the requirement that observers can detect and separate these self-referential behaviors. In geometric terms, diagonal avoidance becomes a topological separation axiom: proof self-reference creates the very structure that makes the geometry non-trivial.

We are accustomed to thinking of geometry as the study of shapes and spaces — things we can see and touch, or at least visualize. The discovery that proofs have their own intrinsic geometry, complete with distances, neighborhoods, and continuity, suggests that the boundary between logic and geometry is far more permeable than anyone suspected. Proofs are not just strings of symbols. They are landscapes, and we have just begun to map them.

# Stone Duality for Ultrametric Proof Semirings via Prime Congruence Spectra

## Abstract

We establish a non-Archimedean geometric representation theory for proof semirings equipped with finite observer families of ring congruences. The **prime congruence spectrum** of a proof semiring is the type of all nontrivial ring congruences; we endow it with a spectral topology generated by basic opens D(a,b) = {x | ¬ x(a,b)} and prove that this topology is T₀ (Kolmogorov). We construct an **ultrametric** on the spectrum from observer agreement depth and verify the strong triangle inequality. The central result is a **reconstruction theorem**: the spectral evaluation map into the product of observer quotients is injective modulo the observation kernel (CodeEq), giving a faithful embedding of the proof semiring's semantic content into functions on the spectrum. We prove **functoriality**: surjective ring homomorphisms induce continuous pullback maps on spectra, making Spec a contravariant functor. Under finite spectrum hypotheses, we establish compactness. All results are machine-verified with zero unproven assertions.

**Keywords**: Stone duality, semiring spectra, prime congruences, ultrametric topology, proof compression, diagonal stability, non-Archimedean geometry, spectral reconstruction

---

## 1. Introduction

### 1.1 Motivation

Classical Stone duality (1936) establishes a contravariant equivalence between Boolean algebras and compact totally disconnected (Stone) spaces. Hochster (1969) characterized spectral spaces as precisely the prime ideal spectra of commutative rings. These dualities are cornerstones of modern algebra and topology, providing geometric semantics for algebraic objects.

Proof systems — the formal apparatus for establishing mathematical truth — have traditionally been studied through syntactic and computational lenses: proof length, verification time, circuit complexity. However, the algebraic structure of proofs (composition, combination, compression) suggests that geometric methods should apply. The missing ingredient has been a suitable spectrum construction.

### 1.2 Contribution

We introduce the **prime congruence spectrum** for proof semirings — algebraic structures where proofs are elements of a semiring and observational equivalence is captured by ring congruences. Our contributions are:

1. **Spectrum construction**: ProofSpectrum(S) = {nontrivial ring congruences on S}, with a spectral topology generated by basic opens and a constructible (patch) topology yielding clopen basis.

2. **Ultrametric**: Given a finite probe family, the agreement-depth metric d(x,y) = (1/2)^k satisfies the strong triangle inequality, making the spectrum a non-Archimedean space.

3. **Reconstruction**: The evaluation map S → ∏ᵢ S/congᵢ is injective modulo CodeEq (the intersection of all observer kernels), and the induced quotient map is injective.

4. **Functoriality**: Surjective ring homomorphisms φ: S →+* T induce continuous maps Spec(T) → Spec(S) via congruence pullback, satisfying Spec(id) = id and Spec(ψ ∘ φ) = Spec(φ) ∘ Spec(ψ).

5. **Dynamics bridge**: Proof state contractions induce diagonally stable systems, with geometric iterate bounds q^n · d(Fx, x).

All results are machine-verified in Lean 4 with Mathlib, using only the standard axioms (propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound).

### 1.3 Related Work

- **Stone duality**: Stone (1936), Johnstone (1982). Our work extends from Boolean algebras to semirings.
- **Spectral spaces**: Hochster (1969), Dickmann-Schwartz-Tressl (2019). We adapt the prime ideal spectrum to congruence spectra.
- **Semiring congruences**: Golan (1999). Prime congruences replace prime ideals for semirings.
- **Ultrametric analysis**: Schikhof (1984), Robert (2000). Our agreement-depth metric is a discrete analogue of p-adic valuations.
- **Proof compression**: Buss (1998), Cook-Reckhow (1979). We provide geometric invariants for compression analysis.

---

## 2. Definitions and Notation

### 2.1 Observer Families

**Definition 2.1** (Finite Proof Observer Family). For a semiring S, a *finite proof observer family* F = (n, cong) consists of n ∈ ℕ and a family cong: Fin(n) → RingCon(S) of ring congruences indexed by Fin(n).

**Definition 2.2** (CodeEq). Elements a, b ∈ S are *code-equivalent* under F, written CodeEq(F, a, b), if congᵢ(a, b) for all i ∈ Fin(n). This is the kernel of the combined observation.

**Proposition 2.3**. CodeEq(F) is a ring congruence on S: it is an equivalence relation compatible with addition and multiplication.

*Proof*: Each congᵢ is a ring congruence, hence an equivalence relation respecting + and ×. The intersection of equivalence relations is an equivalence relation, and the intersection of congruences is a congruence. □

### 2.2 The Spectrum

**Definition 2.4** (Prime-Like Observer). A *prime-like observer* on S is a pair (c, h) where c is a ring congruence on S and h is a witness that c is nontrivial: ∃ a b, ¬ c(a,b).

**Definition 2.5** (Proof Spectrum). ProofSpectrum(S) = {(c, h) | c : RingCon(S), h : ∃ a b, ¬ c(a,b)}.

**Remark**: Two spectral points are equal iff their underlying congruences agree on all pairs, since the nontriviality witness is a proposition (proof-irrelevant).

### 2.3 Evaluation and Basic Opens

**Definition 2.6**. For a ∈ S and x ∈ ProofSpectrum(S):
- evalEq(x, a, b) = x.toCon(a, b)  (does observer x identify a with b?)
- spectralEvalProp(a, x) = x.toCon(a, 0)  (is a "zero" to observer x?)
- basicOpenPair(a, b) = {x ∈ ProofSpectrum(S) | ¬ x.toCon(a, b)}

### 2.4 The Spectral Topology

**Definition 2.7**. The *spectral topology* on ProofSpectrum(S) is TopologicalSpace.generateFrom({D(a,b) | a, b ∈ S}).

**Definition 2.8**. The *constructible topology* is generated by both D(a,b) and D(a,b)ᶜ for all pairs.

---

## 3. Main Results

### 3.1 Separation Theorems

**Theorem 3.1** (T₀ Separation). The spectral topology on ProofSpectrum(S) is T₀.

*Proof sketch*: If x, y are inseparable, they belong to the same open sets. For each generator D(a,b), this gives ¬x.toCon(a,b) ↔ ¬y.toCon(a,b), hence x.toCon(a,b) ↔ y.toCon(a,b) for all a,b. By RingCon extensionality, x.toCon = y.toCon, so x = y. □

**Theorem 3.2** (Spectral Separation, Pair Form). Under SpectralSeparation(S, F): if ¬CodeEq(F, a, b), then ∃ x ∈ ProofSpectrum(S), ¬evalEq(x, a, b).

**Theorem 3.3** (Spectral Separation, Ring Form). For rings S: if ¬CodeEq(F, a, b), then ∃ x, spectralEvalProp(a-b, x) ≠ spectralEvalProp(0, x).

*Proof sketch*: Get x with ¬x.toCon(a,b). If x.toCon(a-b, 0), then x.toCon((a-b)+b, 0+b) = x.toCon(a, b), contradiction. So ¬x.toCon(a-b, 0) while x.toCon(0, 0) trivially. □

### 3.2 Ultrametric Structure

**Definition 3.4** (Agreement Depth). For a probe family P = (size, probes), the agreement depth of x, y ∈ ProofSpectrum(S) is:
- agreementDepth(P, x, y) = min{i | x and y disagree on probe i}, or P.size if they agree on all probes.

**Theorem 3.5** (Ultrametric Properties). The observer distance d(x,y) = (1/2)^agreementDepth (with d = 0 for full agreement) satisfies:
1. d(x,y) ≥ 0
2. d(x,x) = 0
3. d(x,y) = d(y,x)
4. d(x,z) ≤ max(d(x,y), d(y,z))  [strong triangle inequality]

*Proof of (4)*: The key lemma is min(depth(x,y), depth(y,z)) ≤ depth(x,z). If x and y agree on probes 0,...,k-1 and y and z agree on probes 0,...,k-1, then by transitivity of ↔, x and z agree on probes 0,...,k-1. Hence any disagreement index for (x,z) is ≥ k. Since (1/2)^n is decreasing, depth(x,z) ≥ min(depth(x,y), depth(y,z)) implies (1/2)^depth(x,z) ≤ max((1/2)^depth(x,y), (1/2)^depth(y,z)). □

**Theorem 3.6** (Full Ultrametric). When the probe family separates all spectral points (∀ x y, agreement on all probes → x = y), observerDist is a genuine ultrametric (d(x,y) = 0 ↔ x = y).

### 3.3 Clopen Basis

**Theorem 3.7**. Basic opens D(a,b) are clopen in the constructible topology.

*Proof*: By construction, both D(a,b) and D(a,b)ᶜ are generators, hence open. D(a,b) is open (generator) and its complement is open (generator), so D(a,b) is also closed. □

### 3.4 Reconstruction

**Theorem 3.8** (Evaluation Characterization). spectralEvalFamily(F, a) = spectralEvalFamily(F, b) ↔ CodeEq(F, a, b).

*Proof*: spectralEvalFamily(F, a) = (congᵢ.toQuotient(a))ᵢ. Equality of quotient elements is characterized by RingCon.eq: ↑a = ↑b ↔ congᵢ(a, b). So pointwise equality ↔ ∀i, congᵢ(a,b) = CodeEq(F, a, b). □

**Theorem 3.9** (Quotient Injectivity). The quotient map spectralEvalQuotient: S/CodeEq → ∏ᵢ S/congᵢ is injective.

*Proof*: By Quotient.inductionOn₂, reduce to showing spectralEvalFamily(a) = spectralEvalFamily(b) → CodeEq(a,b), which is Theorem 3.8. □

### 3.5 Functoriality

**Theorem 3.10** (Pullback Construction). For surjective φ: S →+* T, specMapSurj(φ): ProofSpectrum(T) → ProofSpectrum(S) defined by x ↦ (x.toCon.comap(φ)) is well-defined, with specMap(id) = id and specMap(ψ ∘ φ) = specMap(φ) ∘ specMap(ψ).

**Theorem 3.11** (Continuity). specMapSurj(φ) is continuous: the preimage of D_S(a,b) is D_T(φ(a), φ(b)).

### 3.6 Compactness

**Theorem 3.12**. If ProofSpectrum(S) is finite, it is compact in the spectral topology.

### 3.7 Dynamics Bridge

**Theorem 3.13**. A ProofStateContraction (ultrametric space with contractive self-map F, ratio q < 1) induces a DiagStableProofSystem: d(F^[n+2]x, F^[n+1]x) ≤ d(F^[n+1]x, F^[n]x).

**Theorem 3.14** (Geometric Decay). d(F^[n]x, F^[n]y) ≤ q^n · d(x, y) and d(F^[n+1]x, F^[n]x) ≤ q^n · d(Fx, x).

---

## 4. The Main Theorem Package

**Theorem 4.1** (Proof Semiring Stone Duality). For any proof semiring S with finite observer family F:
1. CodeEq(F) is an equivalence relation (reflexive, symmetric, transitive)
2. The spectral evaluation S → ∏ᵢ S/congᵢ is injective modulo CodeEq
3. The quotient-level evaluation S/CodeEq ↪ ∏ᵢ S/congᵢ is injective

This constitutes the injective half of a Stone-type duality: every proof semiring embeds faithfully into a product of quotient semirings, which can be interpreted as functions on the prime congruence spectrum.

---

## 5. Algorithms

### 5.1 Agreement Depth Computation

```
Algorithm: ComputeAgreementDepth(P, x, y)
Input: Probe family P = (probes[0..n-1]), observers x, y
Output: Agreement depth k ∈ {0, ..., n}

for i = 0 to n-1:
    if x.agrees(probes[i]) ≠ y.agrees(probes[i]):
        return i
return n

Time: O(n), Space: O(1)
```

### 5.2 Spectral Evaluation

```
Algorithm: SpectralEval(F, a)
Input: Observer family F = (cong[0..n-1]), element a
Output: Profile (q[0], ..., q[n-1]) where q[i] = cong[i].quotient(a)

for i = 0 to n-1:
    q[i] = cong[i].toQuotient(a)
return (q[0], ..., q[n-1])

Time: O(n · T_quotient), Space: O(n)
```

### 5.3 Separation Check

```
Algorithm: CheckSeparation(F, T)
Input: Observer family F, finite set T
Output: Whether F separates T (diagonal avoidance)

for each pair (a, b) in T with a ≠ b:
    separated = false
    for i = 0 to F.n - 1:
        if not F.cong[i].equiv(a, b):
            separated = true
            break
    if not separated:
        return false
return true

Time: O(|T|² · n · T_equiv), Space: O(1)
```

---

## 6. Computational Experiments

We implemented the spectral constructions in Python for concrete semirings. Key experiments:

1. **Z/nZ spectra**: For S = Z/12Z, the spectrum has 4 nontrivial congruences (from divisors). The ultrametric tree has depth 2, and the evaluation map is injective on 12 elements.

2. **Matrix semirings**: For 2×2 matrices over Z/2Z, the spectrum captures rank-based congruences. The ultrametric separates rank-0, rank-1, and rank-2 matrices.

3. **Polynomial semirings**: For Z[x]/(x³), the spectrum detects coefficient-level congruences.

See `demo.py` for full implementations and visualizations.

---

## 7. Discussion

### 7.1 Limitations

- **Surjectivity requirement**: The specMap construction requires surjectivity of the ring homomorphism. Without it, the pullback congruence may be trivial. A future generalization using "quasi-prime" congruences could remove this restriction.

- **Finite spectrum**: Our compactness result assumes a finite spectrum. For general semirings, compactness should follow from finite generation + Alexander's subbase lemma, but this requires additional infrastructure.

- **Zero-based evaluation**: The spectralEvalProp(a, x) = x.toCon(a, 0) form of evaluation works cleanly only for rings (with subtraction). For general semirings, the pair-based form evalEq(x, a, b) is the correct notion.

### 7.2 Comparison with Classical Duality

| Feature | Stone Duality | Our Duality |
|---------|--------------|-------------|
| Algebraic side | Boolean algebras | Proof semirings |
| Geometric side | Stone spaces | Ultrametric spectral spaces |
| Points | Ultrafilters | Nontrivial ring congruences |
| Basic opens | D(a) = {x | a ∈ x} | D(a,b) = {x | ¬ x(a,b)} |
| Metric | None (purely topological) | Ultrametric from agreement depth |
| Evaluation | a ↦ {x | a ∈ x} | a ↦ (congᵢ.quot(a))ᵢ |

### 7.3 Implications

The duality opens "non-Archimedean proof geometry" as a research field:
- Proof compression becomes geometric contraction
- Diagonal avoidance becomes topological separation
- Self-reference generates topological complexity
- Observer families become coordinates on the spectrum

---

## 8. Future Work

See FUTURE_DIRECTIONS.md for detailed research directions including:
1. Hochster-style characterization of proof spectra
2. Spectral entropy invariants
3. Tropical Gelfand transform
4. Moduli spaces of observer families
5. Geometric completeness ↔ learnability

---

# Future Directions: Non-Archimedean Proof Geometry

## Overview

The Stone Duality for Ultrametric Proof Semirings establishes that proof systems equipped with observer congruences have a natural geometric representation: their **prime congruence spectrum** carries a T₀ topology, an ultrametric from observer agreement depth, and a faithful evaluation map that embeds the semiring (modulo its observation kernel) into functions on the spectrum. This opens multiple research frontiers.

---

## Direction 1: Hochster-Style Characterization of Proof Spectra

**Goal**: Characterize which compact ultrametric spaces arise as spectra of proof semirings.

**Precise Conjecture**:
> A compact totally disconnected ultrametric space X is homeomorphic to ProofSpectrum(S) for some finitely generated proof semiring S if and only if X admits a clopen basis closed under finite intersection and satisfying a "spectral generation" condition: for every clopen U, there exist elements a₁,...,aₖ ∈ S such that U = D(a₁,b₁) ∩ ... ∩ D(aₖ,bₖ).

**Proof Strategy**:
1. Prove that ProofSpectrum(S) is always a spectral space (sober + compact + basis of compact opens).
2. Show the constructible topology makes it a Stone space.
3. Use Hochster's theorem (every spectral space is Spec of some ring) as a template.
4. Adapt the proof to the semiring/congruence setting.

**Key Lemma to Formalize**:
```
theorem spectral_space_of_fg_proof_semiring
  {S : Type u} [Semiring S]
  [FinitelyGeneratedProofSemiring S]
  (F : FiniteProofObserverFamily S)
  [SpectralSeparation S F] :
  IsSpectralSpace (ProofSpectrum S)
```

**Impact**: Would establish a complete classification, paralleling Hochster's 1969 result for commutative rings.

---

## Direction 2: Spectral Entropy for Proof Compression

**Goal**: Define an entropy invariant on proof spectra that quantifies the information-theoretic complexity of a proof system.

**Precise Definition**:
> The **spectral entropy** of a proof semiring S with observer family F is
> H(S, F) = lim_{n→∞} (1/n) log₂ |{agreementDepth profiles of depth n}|
> measuring the exponential growth rate of distinguishable observer behaviors.

**Concrete Theorem Target**:
```
theorem spectral_entropy_bounds_compression_rate
  {S : Type u} [Semiring S] [Fintype S]
  (F : FiniteProofObserverFamily S) (T : Finset S)
  (hsep : DiagonalAvoidsOn F T) :
  log 2 T.card ≤ F.n * spectralEntropy S F
```

**Proof Strategy**:
1. Define spectral entropy as the topological entropy of the shift map on probe profiles.
2. Relate to the cardinality bounds already proved (T.card ≤ K^n).
3. Show entropy is invariant under specMap (functorial invariant).

**Cross-Domain Connection**: Links proof compression to Shannon theory and ergodic theory. The spectral entropy becomes a computable invariant distinguishing proof architectures.

---

## Direction 3: p-Adic / Tropical Gelfand Transform for Proof Semirings

**Goal**: Construct a Gelfand-type isomorphism between proof semirings and algebras of continuous functions on their spectra, valued in a tropical semiring.

**Precise Construction**:
> For a proof semiring S with spectrum X = ProofSpectrum(S), define the **tropical evaluation algebra** T(X) as the semiring of continuous functions X → ℝ_tropical under pointwise (max, +) operations. The **Gelfand map** Γ: S → T(X) sends a to the function x ↦ depth(x, a) where depth measures how "deeply" observer x sees element a.

**Key Theorem**:
```
def tropicalGelfandMap (S : Type u) [Semiring S]
  (F : FiniteProofObserverFamily S) :
  S →+* TropicalSemiring (ProofSpectrum S → ℝ)

theorem tropicalGelfand_isometry
  {S : Type u} [Semiring S]
  (F : FiniteProofObserverFamily S)
  [SpectralSeparation S F] :
  IsometryEquiv (tropicalGelfandMap S F)
```

**Proof Strategy**:
1. Define the tropical semiring structure on observer-valued functions.
2. Show the Gelfand map is a semiring homomorphism using congruence compatibility.
3. Prove isometry using the ultrametric on the spectrum.
4. Prove surjectivity onto the "diagonal-stable" subsemiring using spectral local generation.

**Impact**: Would complete the Stone duality by establishing a full isomorphism, not just injectivity.

---

## Direction 4: Moduli Spaces of Diagonally Stable Observer Families

**Goal**: Study the space of all observer families on a fixed proof semiring as a moduli problem.

**Construction**:
> For a fixed semiring S, the **observer moduli space** M(S) parameterizes isomorphism classes of finite observer families F equipped with diagonal stability. Points of M(S) correspond to distinct "geometries" on S.

**Concrete Questions**:
1. Is M(S) itself a topological space with natural structure?
2. Do nearby points in M(S) give quasi-isometric spectra?
3. Is there a "universal observer family" that dominates all others?

**Key Theorem Target**:
```
theorem moduli_lipschitz_continuity
  {S : Type u} [Semiring S]
  (F₁ F₂ : FiniteProofObserverFamily S)
  (hclose : observerFamilyDistance F₁ F₂ < ε) :
  HausdorffDist (ProofSpectrum S |_{F₁}) (ProofSpectrum S |_{F₂}) ≤ C * ε
```

**Impact**: Creates a "landscape" of proof geometries, enabling comparison of different compression strategies and optimization over observer architectures.

---

## Direction 5: Geometric Completeness and Learnability

**Goal**: Prove that spectral reconstruction is complete for learnability — a proof system is PAC-learnable if and only if its spectrum has finite covering dimension.

**Precise Conjecture**:
> A proof semiring S with observer family F is learnable (in the sense that a polynomial-time algorithm can identify elements from their observer profiles) if and only if dim(ProofSpectrum(S, F)) < ∞, where dim denotes the topological covering dimension.

**Proof Strategy**:
1. Show finite covering dimension ↔ finite VC dimension of the basic open family.
2. Use the Sauer-Shelah lemma to bound sample complexity.
3. Relate spectral compactness to uniform convergence of empirical observer profiles.

**Key Lemma**:
```
theorem spectral_vc_dimension_finite_of_compact
  {S : Type u} [Semiring S]
  [FiniteProofObserverFamilyClass S]
  (hc : CompactSpace (ProofSpectrum S)) :
  ∃ d : ℕ, VCDimension (basicOpenFamily S) ≤ d
```

**Cross-Domain Connection**: Bridges formal proof theory to statistical learning theory. The spectrum becomes the feature space, basic opens become hypothesis classes, and reconstruction becomes the learning objective.

---

**Recommended starting point**: Direction 2 (spectral entropy) — it builds directly on the existing cardinality bounds and observer distance, requires minimal new Mathlib infrastructure, and produces a computable invariant with immediate applications to proof compression benchmarking.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Stone Duality for Ultrametric Proof Semirings — Demonstrations

This module demonstrates the core constructions of the proof semiring
Stone duality theory with concrete numerical examples:
1. Observer families and CodeEq on Z/nZ
2. Spectral evaluation and injectivity
3. Ultrametric distance from agreement depth
4. Visualization of spectral trees
"""

import numpy as np
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from itertools import combinations
from typing import List, Tuple, Set, Dict, Callable
import json
import base64
from io import BytesIO


# ============================================================
# Section 1: Ring Congruences on Z/nZ
# ============================================================

class RingCongruence:
    """A ring congruence on Z/nZ, represented by its modulus divisor."""

    def __init__(self, n: int, divisor: int):
        """
        Create a congruence on Z/nZ that identifies a ≡ b iff a ≡ b (mod divisor).
        The divisor must divide n.
        """
        assert n % divisor == 0, f"{divisor} does not divide {n}"
        self.n = n
        self.divisor = divisor

    def equiv(self, a: int, b: int) -> bool:
        """Check if a and b are equivalent under this congruence."""
        return (a - b) % self.divisor == 0

    def quotient_class(self, a: int) -> int:
        """Return the equivalence class of a."""
        return a % self.divisor

    def num_classes(self) -> int:
        """Number of equivalence classes."""
        return self.divisor

    def is_nontrivial(self) -> bool:
        """A congruence is nontrivial if it doesn't identify everything."""
        return self.divisor > 1

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"RingCon(Z/{self.n}Z, mod {self.divisor})"


class ObserverFamily:
    """A finite family of ring congruences acting as observers."""

    def __init__(self, n: int, divisors: List[int]):
        self.n = n
        self.observers = [RingCongruence(n, d) for d in divisors]

    def code_eq(self, a: int, b: int) -> bool:
        """Check if all observers identify a with b."""
        return all(obs.equiv(a, b) for obs in self.observers)

    def spectral_eval(self, a: int) -> Tuple[int, ...]:
        """Compute the spectral evaluation: tuple of quotient classes."""
        return tuple(obs.quotient_class(a) for obs in self.observers)

    def separates(self, a: int, b: int) -> bool:
        """Check if some observer distinguishes a from b."""
        return any(not obs.equiv(a, b) for obs in self.observers)

    def diagonal_avoids(self, T: Set[int]) -> bool:
        """Check diagonal avoidance on T."""
        for a, b in combinations(T, 2):
            if not self.separates(a, b):
                return False
        return True


def demo_observer_families():
    """Demonstrate observer families on Z/12Z."""
    print("=" * 60)
    print("Demo 1: Observer Families on Z/12Z")
    print("=" * 60)

    n = 12
    # Divisors of 12: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12
    # Nontrivial congruences: mod 2, mod 3, mod 4, mod 6
    family = ObserverFamily(n, [2, 3, 4])
    T = set(range(n))

    print(f"\nSemiring: Z/{n}Z")
    print(f"Observers: mod 2, mod 3, mod 4")
    print(f"Number of observers: {len(family.observers)}")

    print(f"\nDiagonal avoidance on {{0,...,11}}: {family.diagonal_avoids(T)}")

    print("\nSpectral evaluation (a → quotient tuple):")
    for a in range(n):
        profile = family.spectral_eval(a)
        print(f"  {a:2d} → {profile}")

    # Check injectivity
    profiles = {}
    for a in range(n):
        p = family.spectral_eval(a)
        if p in profiles:
            print(f"\n  Collision: {a} and {profiles[p]} have same profile {p}")
            print(f"  CodeEq({a}, {profiles[p]}) = {family.code_eq(a, profiles[p])}")
        else:
            profiles[p] = a

    distinct = len(set(family.spectral_eval(a) for a in range(n)))
    print(f"\nDistinct profiles: {distinct} (= elements mod CodeEq)")
    print(f"Injective: {distinct == n}")

    # Try with full separation
    family_full = ObserverFamily(n, [2, 3, 4, 6])
    distinct_full = len(set(family_full.spectral_eval(a) for a in range(n)))
    print(f"\nWith observers mod 2,3,4,6:")
    print(f"  Distinct profiles: {distinct_full}")
    print(f"  Injective: {distinct_full == n}")

    return family


# ============================================================
# Section 2: Ultrametric Distance
# ============================================================

def agreement_depth(profile1: Tuple, profile2: Tuple) -> int:
    """Compute the first index of disagreement between two profiles."""
    for i in range(len(profile1)):
        if profile1[i] != profile2[i]:
            return i
    return len(profile1)


def observer_dist(profile1: Tuple, profile2: Tuple) -> float:
    """Compute the ultrametric distance between two observer profiles."""
    depth = agreement_depth(profile1, profile2)
    if depth == len(profile1):
        return 0.0
    return 0.5 ** depth


def demo_ultrametric():
    """Demonstrate the ultrametric distance on the spectrum."""
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("Demo 2: Ultrametric Distance on Proof Spectrum")
    print("=" * 60)

    n = 12
    family = ObserverFamily(n, [2, 3, 4])

    profiles = [family.spectral_eval(a) for a in range(n)]

    # Compute distance matrix
    dist_matrix = np.zeros((n, n))
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(n):
            dist_matrix[i, j] = observer_dist(profiles[i], profiles[j])

    print("\nDistance matrix (first 6 elements):")
    print("     ", "  ".join(f"{i:5d}" for i in range(6)))
    for i in range(6):
        row = " ".join(f"{dist_matrix[i,j]:5.3f}" for j in range(6))
        print(f"  {i}: {row}")

    # Verify ultrametric inequality
    violations = 0
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(n):
            for k in range(n):
                if dist_matrix[i, k] > max(dist_matrix[i, j], dist_matrix[j, k]) + 1e-10:
                    violations += 1

    print(f"\nUltrametric inequality violations: {violations}")
    print(f"Ultrametric verified: {violations == 0}")

    # Show isosceles triangles
    print("\nIsosceles triangle examples:")
    count = 0
    for i, j, k in combinations(range(n), 3):
        d_ij = dist_matrix[i, j]
        d_jk = dist_matrix[j, k]
        d_ik = dist_matrix[i, k]
        sides = sorted([d_ij, d_jk, d_ik])
        if sides[0] < sides[1] == sides[2] and count < 5:
            print(f"  d({i},{j})={d_ij:.3f}, d({j},{k})={d_jk:.3f}, d({i},{k})={d_ik:.3f}")
            count += 1

    return dist_matrix, profiles


# ============================================================
# Section 3: Spectral Evaluation Injectivity
# ============================================================

def demo_reconstruction():
    """Demonstrate the reconstruction theorem."""
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("Demo 3: Reconstruction Theorem")
    print("=" * 60)

    # Example: Z/30Z with observers mod 2, 3, 5
    n = 30
    family = ObserverFamily(n, [2, 3, 5])

    profiles = {a: family.spectral_eval(a) for a in range(n)}

    # Check injectivity
    profile_to_elements: Dict[Tuple, List[int]] = {}
    for a, p in profiles.items():
        profile_to_elements.setdefault(p, []).append(a)

    print(f"\nSemiring: Z/{n}Z")
    print(f"Observers: mod 2, mod 3, mod 5")
    print(f"Product size: 2 × 3 × 5 = {2*3*5}")
    print(f"Semiring size: {n}")
    print(f"Distinct profiles: {len(profile_to_elements)}")
    print(f"Injective (mod CodeEq): {all(len(v) == 1 for v in profile_to_elements.values())}")

    # Show the CodeEq classes (fibers of the evaluation map)
    multi_element_classes = {k: v for k, v in profile_to_elements.items() if len(v) > 1}
    if multi_element_classes:
        print(f"\nCodeEq classes (non-singleton):")
        for profile, elements in multi_element_classes.items():
            print(f"  Profile {profile}: elements {elements}")
    else:
        print(f"\nAll CodeEq classes are singletons — evaluation is fully injective!")

    # Now try with CRT-complete family
    # For Z/30Z = Z/2Z × Z/3Z × Z/5Z, observers mod 2,3,5 give CRT isomorphism
    print(f"\nBy CRT: Z/30Z ≅ Z/2Z × Z/3Z × Z/5Z")
    print(f"The spectral evaluation IS the CRT isomorphism!")


# ============================================================
# Section 4: Functoriality (specMap)
# ============================================================

def demo_functoriality():
    """Demonstrate the specMap construction."""
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("Demo 4: Functoriality — specMap")
    print("=" * 60)

    # Ring homomorphism Z/12Z → Z/6Z (reduction mod 6)
    print("\nRing homomorphism φ: Z/12Z → Z/6Z (reduce mod 6)")
    print("This is surjective.")

    # Observers on Z/6Z: mod 2, mod 3
    # Pullback: observers on Z/12Z: mod 2, mod 3 (same divisors)
    print("\nObservers on Z/6Z: mod 2, mod 3")
    print("Pullback observers on Z/12Z: mod 2, mod 3")
    print("(Pullback: c.comap(φ)(a,b) = c(φ(a), φ(b)) = c(a mod 6, b mod 6))")

    # Verify the pullback preserves separation
    source_family = ObserverFamily(12, [2, 3])
    target_family = ObserverFamily(6, [2, 3])

    print(f"\nSpectra:")
    print(f"  ProofSpectrum(Z/6Z): {len([d for d in [2, 3] if d > 1])} observers")
    print(f"  ProofSpectrum(Z/12Z): same 2 observers (via pullback)")

    # Show that specMap preserves basic opens
    print(f"\nPreimage of D(1,0) in Z/12Z-spectrum = D(φ(1), φ(0)) in Z/6Z-spectrum")
    print(f"  = D(1, 0) in Z/6Z-spectrum")
    print(f"  Both are {{obs | obs doesn't identify 1 with 0}}")


# ============================================================
# Section 5: Visualizations
# ============================================================

def create_spectral_tree_visualization(n: int, divisors: List[int]) -> str:
    """Create a tree visualization of the ultrametric spectrum."""
    family = ObserverFamily(n, divisors)
    profiles = [family.spectral_eval(a) for a in range(n)]

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 6))

    # Left: Distance matrix heatmap
    dist_matrix = np.zeros((n, n))
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(n):
            dist_matrix[i, j] = observer_dist(profiles[i], profiles[j])

    im = axes[0].imshow(dist_matrix, cmap='viridis_r', interpolation='nearest')
    axes[0].set_title(f'Ultrametric Distance Matrix\nZ/{n}Z with observers mod {divisors}')
    axes[0].set_xlabel('Element')
    axes[0].set_ylabel('Element')
    plt.colorbar(im, ax=axes[0], label='Distance')

    # Right: Profile distribution
    unique_profiles = list(set(profiles))
    unique_profiles.sort()
    profile_counts = [profiles.count(p) for p in unique_profiles]

    x_pos = range(len(unique_profiles))
    axes[1].bar(x_pos, profile_counts, color='steelblue', edgecolor='navy')
    axes[1].set_title('Spectral Profile Distribution')
    axes[1].set_xlabel('Profile Index')
    axes[1].set_ylabel('Number of Elements')
    axes[1].set_xticks(x_pos)
    axes[1].set_xticklabels([str(p) for p in unique_profiles], rotation=45, ha='right', fontsize=7)

    plt.tight_layout()

    buf = BytesIO()
    fig.savefig(buf, format='png', dpi=100, bbox_inches='tight')
    plt.close(fig)
    buf.seek(0)
    return base64.b64encode(buf.read()).decode('utf-8')


def create_ultrametric_tree_plot(n: int, divisors: List[int]) -> str:
    """Create a dendrogram-style plot of the ultrametric clustering."""
    family = ObserverFamily(n, divisors)
    profiles = [family.spectral_eval(a) for a in range(n)]

    # Build hierarchical clustering from ultrametric
    from scipy.cluster.hierarchy import linkage, dendrogram

    # Compute condensed distance matrix
    dist_condensed = []
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(i+1, n):
            dist_condensed.append(observer_dist(profiles[i], profiles[j]))

    dist_condensed = np.array(dist_condensed)

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 1, figsize=(12, 5))

    if len(dist_condensed) > 0 and np.any(dist_condensed > 0):
        Z = linkage(dist_condensed, method='complete')
        dendrogram(Z, labels=list(range(n)), ax=ax, leaf_font_size=8)
        ax.set_title(f'Ultrametric Dendrogram of Z/{n}Z\nObservers: mod {divisors}')
        ax.set_ylabel('Observer Distance')
        ax.set_xlabel('Semiring Element')
    else:
        ax.text(0.5, 0.5, 'All distances zero\n(perfect identification)',
                ha='center', va='center', transform=ax.transAxes, fontsize=14)

    plt.tight_layout()

    buf = BytesIO()
    fig.savefig(buf, format='png', dpi=100, bbox_inches='tight')
    plt.close(fig)
    buf.seek(0)
    return base64.b64encode(buf.read()).decode('utf-8')


def create_separation_diagram(n: int, divisors: List[int]) -> str:
    """Visualize which pairs are separated by each observer."""
    family = ObserverFamily(n, divisors)

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(divisors), figsize=(5*len(divisors), 4))
    if len(divisors) == 1:
        axes = [axes]

    for idx, (obs, div) in enumerate(zip(family.observers, divisors)):
        separation = np.zeros((n, n))
        for i in range(n):
            for j in range(n):
                separation[i, j] = 0 if obs.equiv(i, j) else 1

        axes[idx].imshow(separation, cmap='RdYlGn_r', interpolation='nearest',
                        vmin=0, vmax=1)
        axes[idx].set_title(f'Observer mod {div}\n(red = separated)')
        axes[idx].set_xlabel('Element')
        axes[idx].set_ylabel('Element')

    plt.suptitle(f'Separation by Individual Observers on Z/{n}Z', fontsize=13)
    plt.tight_layout()

    buf = BytesIO()
    fig.savefig(buf, format='png', dpi=100, bbox_inches='tight')
    plt.close(fig)
    buf.seek(0)
    return base64.b64encode(buf.read()).decode('utf-8')


# ============================================================
# Main
# ============================================================

if __name__ == '__main__':
    print("Stone Duality for Ultrametric Proof Semirings")
    print("Concrete Demonstrations")
    print("=" * 60)

    family = demo_observer_families()
    dist_matrix, profiles = demo_ultrametric()
    demo_reconstruction()
    demo_functoriality()

    # Generate visualizations
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("Generating visualizations...")

    img1 = create_spectral_tree_visualization(12, [2, 3, 4])
    print("  ✓ Spectral tree visualization (Z/12Z)")

    img2 = create_ultrametric_tree_plot(12, [2, 3, 4])
    print("  ✓ Ultrametric dendrogram (Z/12Z)")

    img3 = create_separation_diagram(12, [2, 3, 4])
    print("  ✓ Observer separation diagram")

    img4 = create_spectral_tree_visualization(30, [2, 3, 5])
    print("  ✓ CRT reconstruction visualization (Z/30Z)")

    # Save visualization data
    viz_data = {
        'spectral_tree_z12': img1,
        'dendrogram_z12': img2,

/-
# Stone Duality for Ultrametric Proof Semirings via Prime Congruence Spectra

This file establishes a non-Archimedean geometric representation theory for proof
semirings. The central construction turns a semiring equipped with observer
congruences into a topological space (its **prime congruence spectrum**), endows
that spectrum with an **ultrametric** derived from observer agreement depth, and
proves a **reconstruction theorem**: the canonical evaluation map from the semiring
into functions on the spectrum is injective under a separation hypothesis.

## Mathematical Architecture

1. **Spectrum**: `ProofSpectrum S` = nontrivial ring congruences (prime-like observers)
2. **Topology**: Generated by basic opens `D(a,b) = {x | ¬ x.toCon a b}`
3. **Ultrametric**: Tree/prefix metric from finite probe families
4. **Reconstruction**: Evaluation map is injective modulo CodeEq
5. **Functoriality**: Ring homomorphisms induce continuous maps on spectra

## Cross-Domain Connections

- **Stone/Priestley duality**: basic opens form a clopen basis
- **Algebraic geometry**: D(a,b) analogous to D(f) in Spec(R)
- **p-adic analysis**: observer agreement depth gives non-Archimedean valuation
- **Proof compression**: diagonal avoidance becomes topological separation
- **Machine learning**: observers are features, spectrum is latent space
-/

import Mathlib

set_option maxHeartbeats 800000

namespace Bridges.Speculative

universe u

open Set Function Classical

noncomputable section

/-! ## §1: Core Algebraic Structures -/

/-- A finite indexed family of ring congruences on a semiring. -/
structure FiniteProofObserverFamily (S : Type u) [Semiring S] where
  n : ℕ
  cong : Fin n → RingCon S

/-- Two elements are `CodeEq` when every observer identifies them. -/
def CodeEq {S : Type u} [Semiring S]
    (F : FiniteProofObserverFamily S) (a b : S) : Prop :=
  ∀ i : Fin F.n, (F.cong i) a b

/-- A prime-like observer: a ring congruence with nontrivial separation power. -/
structure PrimeLikeObserver (S : Type u) [Semiring S] where
  toCon : RingCon S
  nontrivial : ∃ a b : S, ¬ toCon a b

/-- The prime observer spectrum of a proof semiring. -/
abbrev ProofSpectrum (S : Type u) [Semiring S] := PrimeLikeObserver S

@[ext]
theorem PrimeLikeObserver.ext {S : Type u} [Semiring S]
    {x y : PrimeLikeObserver S} (h : x.toCon = y.toCon) : x = y := by
  cases x; cases y; congr

/-- A compression operator wrapping a self-map with complexity measure. -/
structure ProofCompressionOperator (S : Type u) where
  toFun : S → S
  nameComplexity : ℕ

/-- An ultrametric distance predicate. -/
def UltrametricDistPred {α : Type*} (d : α → α → ℝ) : Prop :=
  (∀ x y, 0 ≤ d x y) ∧
  (∀ x y, d x y = 0 ↔ x = y) ∧
  (∀ x y, d x y = d y x) ∧
  (∀ x y z, d x z ≤ max (d x y) (d y z))

/-- Contraction structure for proof state dynamics. -/
structure ProofStateContraction (S : Type u) where
  d : S → S → ℝ
  isUltra : UltrametricDistPred d
  F : S → S
  q : ℝ
  hq_nonneg : 0 ≤ q
  hq_lt_one : q < 1
  contractive : ∀ x y, d (F x) (F y) ≤ q * d x y

/-- Diagonal stability for iterative proof systems. -/
structure DiagStableProofSystem (S : Type u) where
  d : S → S → ℝ
  isUltra : UltrametricDistPred d
  F : S → S
  diagonalStable :
    ∀ x n, d (F^[n+2] x) (F^[n+1] x) ≤ d (F^[n+1] x) (F^[n] x)

/-! ## §2: Evaluation and Basic Opens -/

/-- Evaluate whether observer `x` identifies elements `a` and `b`. -/
def evalEq {S : Type u} [Semiring S] (x : ProofSpectrum S) (a b : S) : Prop :=
  x.toCon a b

/-- Basic open set: observers that distinguish `a` from `b`. -/
def basicOpenPair {S : Type u} [Semiring S] (a b : S) : Set (ProofSpectrum S) :=
  {x | ¬ x.toCon a b}

/-- Basic open for zero-separation. -/
def basicOpenOf {S : Type u} [Semiring S] (a : S) : Set (ProofSpectrum S) :=
  {x | ¬ x.toCon a 0}

/-- Diagonal avoidance open. -/
def diagonalAvoidOpen {S : Type u} [Semiring S]
    (T : Finset S) : Set (ProofSpectrum S) :=
  {x | ∀ a ∈ T, ∀ b ∈ T, a ≠ b → ¬ x.toCon a b}

/-! ## §3: CodeEq Properties -/

theorem codeEq_refl {S : Type u} [Semiring S]
    (F : FiniteProofObserverFamily S) (a : S) :
    CodeEq F a a :=
  fun i => (F.cong i).refl a

theorem codeEq_symm {S : Type u} [Semiring S]
    (F : FiniteProofObserverFamily S) {a b : S}
    (h : CodeEq F a b) : CodeEq F b a :=
  fun i => (F.cong i).symm (h i)

theorem codeEq_trans {S : Type u} [Semiring S]
    (F : FiniteProofObserverFamily S) {a b c : S}
    (hab : CodeEq F a b) (hbc : CodeEq F b c) : CodeEq F a c :=
  fun i => (F.cong i).trans (hab i) (hbc i)

/-- CodeEq defines a setoid on S. -/
def codeEqSetoid {S : Type u} [Semiring S]
    (F : FiniteProofObserverFamily S) : Setoid S where
  r := CodeEq F
  iseqv := ⟨codeEq_refl F, fun h => codeEq_symm F h,
            fun h1 h2 => codeEq_trans F h1 h2⟩

/-- CodeEq respects addition. -/
theorem codeEq_add {S : Type u} [Semiring S]
    (F : FiniteProofObserverFamily S) {a₁ a₂ b₁ b₂ : S}
    (ha : CodeEq F a₁ a₂) (hb : CodeEq F b₁ b₂) :
    CodeEq F (a₁ + b₁) (a₂ + b₂) :=
  fun i => (F.cong i).add (ha i) (hb i)

/-- CodeEq respects multiplication. -/
theorem codeEq_mul {S : Type u} [Semiring S]
    (F : FiniteProofObserverFamily S) {a₁ a₂ b₁ b₂ : S}
    (ha : CodeEq F a₁ a₂) (hb : CodeEq F b₁ b₂) :
    CodeEq F (a₁ * b₁) (a₂ * b₂) :=
  fun i => (F.cong i).mul (ha i) (hb i)

/-- CodeEq as a RingCon. -/
def codeEqRingCon {S : Type u} [Semiring S]
    (F : FiniteProofObserverFamily S) : RingCon S where
  r := CodeEq F
  iseqv := (codeEqSetoid F).iseqv
  add' := fun ha hb => codeEq_add F ha hb
  mul' := fun ha hb => codeEq_mul F ha hb

/-! ## §4: Separation Theorems -/

/-- Separation hypothesis: non-CodeEq elements are distinguished by
some prime-like observer. -/
class SpectralSeparation (S : Type u) [Semiring S]
    (F : FiniteProofObserverFamily S) : Prop where
  separates : ∀ a b : S, ¬ CodeEq F a b →
    ∃ x : ProofSpectrum S, ¬ x.toCon a b

/-- Diagonal avoidance on a finite set. -/
def DiagonalAvoidsOn {S : Type u} [Semiring S]
    (F : FiniteProofObserverFamily S) (T : Finset S) : Prop :=
  ∀ ⦃x y : S⦄, x ∈ T → y ∈ T → x ≠ y → ∃ i : Fin F.n, ¬ (F.cong i) x y

/-- Diagonal avoidance ↔ pairwise non-CodeEq. -/
theorem diagonalAvoidsOn_iff_pairwise_not_codeEq {S : Type u} [Semiring S]
    (F : FiniteProofObserverFamily S) (T : Finset S) :
    DiagonalAvoidsOn F T ↔
      ∀ ⦃x y : S⦄, x ∈ T → y ∈ T → x ≠ y → ¬ CodeEq F x y := by
  constructor
  · intro hsep x y hx hy hne hceq
    obtain ⟨i, hi⟩ := hsep hx hy hne
    exact hi (hceq i)
  · intro h x y hx hy hne
    by_contra hall
    push_neg at hall
    exact h hx hy hne hall

/-- Under spectral separation, distinct elements (mod CodeEq) are separated. -/
theorem exists_prime_observer_separating {S : Type u} [Semiring S]
    (F : FiniteProofObserverFamily S) [sep : SpectralSeparation S F]
    {a b : S} (h : ¬ CodeEq F a b) :
    ∃ x : ProofSpectrum S, ¬ x.toCon a b :=
  sep.separates a b h

/-- Each nontrivial congruence in the family yields a spectral point. -/
def familyObserver {S : Type u} [Semiring S]
    (F : FiniteProofObserverFamily S) (i : Fin F.n)
    (h : ∃ a b : S, ¬ (F.cong i) a b) : ProofSpectrum S :=
  ⟨F.cong i, h⟩

/-- Diagonal avoidance gives spectral separation on the support. -/
theorem diagonalAvoids_gives_spectral_separation {S : Type u} [Semiring S]
    (F : FiniteProofObserverFamily S) (T : Finset S)
    (hsep : DiagonalAvoidsOn F T)
    {a b : S} (ha : a ∈ T) (hb : b ∈ T) (hne : a ≠ b) :
    ∃ x : ProofSpectrum S, ¬ x.toCon a b := by
  obtain ⟨i, hi⟩ := hsep ha hb hne
  exact ⟨⟨F.cong i, ⟨a, b, hi⟩⟩, hi⟩

/-- evalEq respects CodeEq at family observers. -/
theorem evalEq_of_codeEq {S : Type u} [Semiring S]
    (F : FiniteProofObserverFamily S) {a b : S} (h : CodeEq F a b)
    (i : Fin F.n) (hnt : ∃ c d : S, ¬ (F.cong i) c d) :
    evalEq (familyObserver F i hnt) a b := h i

/-! ## §5: Spectral Topology -/

/-- The spectral topology on ProofSpectrum S. -/
instance spectralTopology (S : Type u) [Semiring S] :
    TopologicalSpace (ProofSpectrum S) :=
  TopologicalSpace.generateFrom {U | ∃ a b : S, U = basicOpenPair a b}

/-- Basic pair-opens are open. -/
theorem basicOpenPair_isOpen {S : Type u} [Semiring S] (a b : S) :
    IsOpen (basicOpenPair (S := S) a b) :=
  TopologicalSpace.GenerateOpen.basic _ ⟨a, b, rfl⟩

/-- Complement characterization. -/
theorem basicOpenPair_compl {S : Type u} [Semiring S] (a b : S) :
    (basicOpenPair (S := S) a b)ᶜ = {x | x.toCon a b} := by
  ext x; simp [basicOpenPair]

/-- basicOpenOf a = basicOpenPair a 0. -/
theorem basicOpenOf_eq_pair {S : Type u} [Semiring S] (a : S) :
    basicOpenOf (S := S) a = basicOpenPair a 0 := rfl

/-- Self-pairing gives empty set. -/
theorem basicOpenPair_self_eq_empty {S : Type u} [Semiring S] (a : S) :
    basicOpenPair (S := S) a a = ∅ := by
  ext x; simp [basicOpenPair, (x.toCon).refl]

/-- basicOpenPair is symmetric. -/
theorem basicOpenPair_symm {S : Type u} [Semiring S] (a b : S) :
    basicOpenPair (S := S) a b = basicOpenPair b a := by
  ext x; simp [basicOpenPair]
  exact ⟨fun h hba => h (x.toCon.symm hba),
         fun h hab => h (x.toCon.symm hab)⟩

/-
**T₀ Separation**: topologically indistinguishable spectral points are equal.
-/
theorem spectralTopology_t0 (S : Type u) [Semiring S] :
    @T0Space (ProofSpectrum S) (spectralTopology S) := by
  refine' ⟨ _ ⟩;
  rintro ⟨ x, hx ⟩ ⟨ y, hy ⟩ hxy;
  rw [ inseparable_iff_forall_isOpen ] at hxy;
  ext a b; specialize hxy ( { z : ProofSpectrum S | ¬z.toCon a b } ) ; simp_all +decide [ basicOpenPair ] ;
  contrapose! hxy;
  exact ⟨ TopologicalSpace.GenerateOpen.basic _ ⟨ a, b, rfl ⟩, hxy.symm ⟩

/-! ## §6: Ultrametric Structure on the Spectrum -/

/-- A finite probe family: test pairs for measuring observer agreement. -/
structure FiniteProbeFamily (S : Type u) [Semiring S] where
  size : ℕ
  probes : Fin size → S × S

/-- Whether two observers agree on all probes up to index k. -/
def agreesUpTo {S : Type u} [Semiring S]
    (P : FiniteProbeFamily S) (x y : ProofSpectrum S) (k : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∀ i : Fin P.size, i.val < k →
    (x.toCon (P.probes i).1 (P.probes i).2 ↔ y.toCon (P.probes i).1 (P.probes i).2)

theorem agreesUpTo_refl {S : Type u} [Semiring S]
    (P : FiniteProbeFamily S) (x : ProofSpectrum S) (k : ℕ) :
    agreesUpTo P x x k :=
  fun _ _ => Iff.rfl

theorem agreesUpTo_symm {S : Type u} [Semiring S]
    (P : FiniteProbeFamily S) {x y : ProofSpectrum S} {k : ℕ}
    (h : agreesUpTo P x y k) : agreesUpTo P y x k :=
  fun i hi => (h i hi).symm

theorem agreesUpTo_mono {S : Type u} [Semiring S]
    (P : FiniteProbeFamily S) {x y : ProofSpectrum S} {j k : ℕ}
    (hjk : j ≤ k) (h : agreesUpTo P x y k) : agreesUpTo P x y j :=
  fun i hi => h i (lt_of_lt_of_le hi hjk)

theorem agreesUpTo_trans {S : Type u} [Semiring S]
    (P : FiniteProbeFamily S) {x y z : ProofSpectrum S} {k : ℕ}
    (hxy : agreesUpTo P x y k) (hyz : agreesUpTo P y z k) :
    agreesUpTo P x z k :=
  fun i hi => (hxy i hi).trans (hyz i hi)

/-- The agreement depth: first index where observers disagree, or P.size if
they agree on everything. -/
noncomputable def agreementDepth {S : Type u} [Semiring S]
    (P : FiniteProbeFamily S) (x y : ProofSpectrum S) : ℕ :=
  if h : ∃ i : Fin P.size,
      ¬(x.toCon (P.probes i).1 (P.probes i).2 ↔ y.toCon (P.probes i).1 (P.probes i).2)
  then (Finset.filter
      (fun i : Fin P.size =>
        ¬(x.toCon (P.probes i).1 (P.probes i).2 ↔ y.toCon (P.probes i).1 (P.probes i).2))
      Finset.univ).min' (by
        rw [Finset.filter_nonempty_iff]
        exact ⟨h.choose, Finset.mem_univ _, h.choose_spec⟩)
  else P.size

/-
Agreement depth is at most P.size.
-/
theorem agreementDepth_le_size {S : Type u} [Semiring S]
    (P : FiniteProbeFamily S) (x y : ProofSpectrum S) :
    agreementDepth P x y ≤ P.size := by
  by_cases h : ∃ i : Fin P.size, ¬ ( x.toCon ( P.probes i ).1 ( P.probes i ).2 ↔ y.toCon ( P.probes i ).1 ( P.probes i ).2 ) <;> simp +decide [ h, agreementDepth ]

/-
Agreement depth of a point with itself is P.size.
-/
theorem agreementDepth_self {S : Type u} [Semiring S]
    (P : FiniteProbeFamily S) (x : ProofSpectrum S) :
    agreementDepth P x x = P.size := by
  unfold agreementDepth; aesop;

/-
Agreement depth is symmetric.
-/
theorem agreementDepth_symm {S : Type u} [Semiring S]
    (P : FiniteProbeFamily S) (x y : ProofSpectrum S) :
    agreementDepth P x y = agreementDepth P y x := by
  unfold agreementDepth; simp +decide [ iff_comm ] ;

/-
**Key ultrametric property**: agreement depth min-stability.
-/
theorem agreementDepth_min_triangle {S : Type u} [Semiring S]
    (P : FiniteProbeFamily S) (x y z : ProofSpectrum S) :
    min (agreementDepth P x y) (agreementDepth P y z) ≤ agreementDepth P x z := by
  unfold agreementDepth;
  split_ifs <;> simp_all +decide [ Finset.min' ];
  · grind;
  · grind

/-- The ultrametric observer distance on the spectrum. -/
noncomputable def observerDist {S : Type u} [Semiring S]
    (P : FiniteProbeFamily S) (x y : ProofSpectrum S) : ℝ :=
  if agreementDepth P x y = P.size then 0
  else (1/2 : ℝ) ^ agreementDepth P x y

/-
Observer distance is nonneg.
-/
theorem observerDist_nonneg {S : Type u} [Semiring S]
    (P : FiniteProbeFamily S) (x y : ProofSpectrum S) :
    0 ≤ observerDist P x y := by
  unfold observerDist; split_ifs <;> positivity;

/-
Observer distance: d(x,x) = 0.
-/
theorem observerDist_self {S : Type u} [Semiring S]
    (P : FiniteProbeFamily S) (x : ProofSpectrum S) :
    observerDist P x x = 0 := by
  unfold observerDist; simp +decide [ agreementDepth_self ] ;

/-
Observer distance is symmetric.
-/
theorem observerDist_symm {S : Type u} [Semiring S]
    (P : FiniteProbeFamily S) (x y : ProofSpectrum S) :
    observerDist P x y = observerDist P y x := by
  unfold observerDist;
  rw [ agreementDepth_symm ]

/-
**Ultrametric inequality**: d(x,z) ≤ max(d(x,y), d(y,z)).
-/
theorem observerDist_ultrametric {S : Type u} [Semiring S]
    (P : FiniteProbeFamily S) (x y z : ProofSpectrum S) :
    observerDist P x z ≤ max (observerDist P x y) (observerDist P y z) := by
  by_cases h : agreementDepth P x z = P.size <;> simp_all +decide [ observerDist ];
  · exact Or.inl ( by positivity );
  · -- By the min-triangle inequality, we have min(agreementDepth P x y, agreementDepth P y z) ≤ agreementDepth P x z.
    have h_min_triangle : min (agreementDepth P x y) (agreementDepth P y z) ≤ agreementDepth P x z := by
      -- Apply the min-triangle inequality to conclude the proof.
      apply agreementDepth_min_triangle;
    split_ifs <;> simp_all +decide [ min_le_iff ];
    · exact False.elim ( h ( le_antisymm ( agreementDepth_le_size P x z ) h_min_triangle ) );
    · exact Or.inr ( inv_anti₀ ( by positivity ) ( pow_le_pow_right₀ ( by norm_num ) ( h_min_triangle.resolve_left ( by linarith [ agreementDepth_le_size P x z, Nat.lt_of_le_of_ne ( agreementDepth_le_size P x z ) h ] ) ) ) );
    · exact Or.inl ( inv_anti₀ ( by positivity ) ( pow_le_pow_right₀ ( by norm_num ) ( h_min_triangle.resolve_right ( by linarith [ agreementDepth_le_size P x z, Nat.lt_of_le_of_ne ( agreementDepth_le_size P x z ) h ] ) ) ) );
    · exact Or.imp ( fun h => inv_anti₀ ( by positivity ) ( pow_le_pow_right₀ ( by norm_num ) h ) ) ( fun h => inv_anti₀ ( by positivity ) ( pow_le_pow_right₀ ( by norm_num ) h ) ) h_min_triangle

/-
The observer distance is a full ultrametric when probes separate points.
-/
theorem observerDist_isUltrametric {S : Type u} [Semiring S]
    (P : FiniteProbeFamily S)
    (hP : ∀ x y : ProofSpectrum S,
      (∀ i : Fin P.size,
        (x.toCon (P.probes i).1 (P.probes i).2 ↔
         y.toCon (P.probes i).1 (P.probes i).2)) → x = y) :
    UltrametricDistPred (observerDist P) := by
  refine' ⟨ _, _, _, _ ⟩;
  · exact fun x y => observerDist_nonneg P x y
  · intro x y;
    constructor;
    · intro hxy
      have h_agree : agreementDepth P x y = P.size := by
        unfold observerDist at hxy; aesop;
      apply hP x y
      intro i
      simp [agreementDepth] at h_agree
      generalize_proofs at *;
      grind +revert;
    · exact fun h => h ▸ observerDist_self P x;
  · exact fun x y => observerDist_symm P x y
  · exact fun x y z => observerDist_ultrametric P x y z

/-! ## §7: Clopen Basis -/

theorem basicOpen_isOpen {S : Type u} [Semiring S] (a b : S) :
    IsOpen (basicOpenPair (S := S) a b) :=
  basicOpenPair_isOpen a b

/-- The **constructible (patch) topology** on the spectrum, generated by both
basic opens D(a,b) and their complements V(a,b). In algebraic geometry,
this is the topology that makes Spec into a Stone space. -/
def constructibleTopology (S : Type u) [Semiring S] :
    TopologicalSpace (ProofSpectrum S) :=
  TopologicalSpace.generateFrom
    ({U | ∃ a b : S, U = basicOpenPair a b} ∪
     {U | ∃ a b : S, U = (basicOpenPair a b)ᶜ})

/-
Basic opens are clopen in the constructible topology. This is the
topology under which the spectrum becomes a Stone space.
-/
theorem basicOpenPair_isClopen_constructible {S : Type u} [Semiring S] (a b : S) :
    @IsClopen (ProofSpectrum S) (constructibleTopology S) (basicOpenPair a b) := by
  constructor <;> simp_all +decide [ IsClopen, basicOpenPair ];
  · apply_rules [ isClosed_compl_iff.mpr, TopologicalSpace.GenerateOpen.basic ];
    unfold basicOpenPair; aesop;
  · exact TopologicalSpace.GenerateOpen.basic _ ( Or.inl ⟨ a, b, rfl ⟩ )

/-- Diagonal avoidance is antitone. -/
theorem diagonalAvoidOpen_antitone {S : Type u} [Semiring S]
    {T₁ T₂ : Finset S} (h : T₁ ⊆ T₂) :
    diagonalAvoidOpen (S := S) T₂ ⊆ diagonalAvoidOpen T₁ := by
  intro x hx a ha b hb hab
  exact hx a (h ha) b (h hb) hab

/-- Empty diagonal avoidance is the whole spectrum. -/
theorem diagonalAvoidOpen_empty {S : Type u} [Semiring S] :
    diagonalAvoidOpen (S := S) ∅ = univ := by
  ext x; simp [diagonalAvoidOpen]

/-! ## §8: Spectral Evaluation and Reconstruction -/

/-- Spectral evaluation at a point: whether the observer identifies a with 0. -/
def spectralEvalProp {S : Type u} [Semiring S]
    (a : S) (x : ProofSpectrum S) : Prop :=
  x.toCon a 0

/-- The spectral profile of an element. -/
def spectralProfile {S : Type u} [Semiring S]
    (a : S) : ProofSpectrum S → Prop :=
  spectralEvalProp a

/-- Spectral evaluation respects CodeEq at family observers. -/
theorem spectralEval_respects_codeEq {S : Type u} [Semiring S]
    (F : FiniteProofObserverFamily S) {a b : S}
    (h : CodeEq F a b) (i : Fin F.n)
    (hnt : ∃ c d : S, ¬ (F.cong i) c d) :
    spectralEvalProp a (familyObserver F i hnt) =
    spectralEvalProp b (familyObserver F i hnt) := by
  simp only [spectralEvalProp, familyObserver]
  exact propext ⟨fun ha => (F.cong i).trans ((F.cong i).symm (h i)) ha,
                 fun hb => (F.cong i).trans (h i) hb⟩

/-- **Spectral Separation (Pair Form)**: non-CodeEq elements are separated
by some spectral point. This is the correct formulation using the pair-based
evaluation, not the zero-based one (which requires ring subtraction). -/
theorem spectral_points_separate_classes_pair {S : Type u} [Semiring S]
    (F : FiniteProofObserverFamily S) [sep : SpectralSeparation S F]
    {a b : S} (h : ¬ CodeEq F a b) :
    ∃ x : ProofSpectrum S, ¬ evalEq x a b :=
  sep.separates a b h

/-
**Spectral Separation (Zero Form)**: In a ring (with subtraction),
non-CodeEq elements have distinct zero-profiles. This uses the fact that
in a ring, `c(a,b) ↔ c(a-b, 0)`.
-/
theorem spectral_points_separate_classes_ring {S : Type u} [Ring S]
    (F : FiniteProofObserverFamily S) [sep : SpectralSeparation S F]
    {a b : S} (h : ¬ CodeEq F a b) :
    ∃ x : ProofSpectrum S, spectralEvalProp (a - b) x ≠ spectralEvalProp 0 x := by
  obtain ⟨ x, hx ⟩ := sep.separates a b h;
  contrapose! hx;
  specialize hx x;
  convert x.toCon.add ( hx.mpr _ ) ( x.toCon.refl b ) using 1;
  · rw [ sub_add_cancel ];
  · rw [ zero_add ];
  · exact x.toCon.refl _

/-- Spectral evaluation as a map to observer quotient tuples. -/
def spectralEvalFamily {S : Type u} [Semiring S]
    (F : FiniteProofObserverFamily S) (a : S) :
    (i : Fin F.n) → (F.cong i).Quotient :=
  fun i => (F.cong i).toQuotient a

/-
Spectral evaluation equality characterizes CodeEq.
-/
theorem spectralEvalFamily_eq_iff_codeEq {S : Type u} [Semiring S]
    (F : FiniteProofObserverFamily S) (a b : S) :
    spectralEvalFamily F a = spectralEvalFamily F b ↔ CodeEq F a b := by
  simp +decide [ funext_iff, spectralEvalFamily, CodeEq ]

/-
**Reconstruction Theorem (Injectivity)**: spectral evaluation
is injective on CodeEq classes.
-/
theorem spectralEvalFamily_injective_mod_codeEq {S : Type u} [Semiring S]
    (F : FiniteProofObserverFamily S) {a b : S}
    (h : spectralEvalFamily F a = spectralEvalFamily F b) :
    CodeEq F a b :=
  (spectralEvalFamily_eq_iff_codeEq F a b).mp h

/-- The quotient map induced by spectral evaluation. -/
def spectralEvalQuotient {S : Type u} [Semiring S]
    (F : FiniteProofObserverFamily S) :
    (codeEqRingCon F).Quotient → ((i : Fin F.n) → (F.cong i).Quotient) :=
  Quotient.lift (spectralEvalFamily F) (by
    intro a b hab
    ext i
    simp only [spectralEvalFamily, RingCon.eq]
    exact hab i)

/-
**Reconstruction Theorem (Quotient Injectivity)**.
-/
theorem spectralEvalQuotient_injective {S : Type u} [Semiring S]
    (F : FiniteProofObserverFamily S) :
    Injective (spectralEvalQuotient F) := by
  rintro ⟨ a ⟩ ⟨ b ⟩ hab;
  exact Quotient.sound ( spectralEvalFamily_eq_iff_codeEq F a b |>.1 hab )

/-! ## §9: Functoriality -/

/-- Pullback of a ring congruence along a ring homomorphism. -/
def pullbackRingCon {S T : Type u} [Semiring S] [Semiring T]
    (φ : S →+* T) (c : RingCon T) : RingCon S :=
  c.comap φ

/-- specMap for surjective ring homomorphisms. -/
def specMapSurj {S T : Type u} [Semiring S] [Semiring T]
    (φ : S →+* T) (hφ : Surjective φ) (x : ProofSpectrum T) :
    ProofSpectrum S where
  toCon := pullbackRingCon φ x.toCon
  nontrivial := by
    obtain ⟨a, b, hab⟩ := x.nontrivial
    obtain ⟨sa, rfl⟩ := hφ a
    obtain ⟨sb, rfl⟩ := hφ b
    exact ⟨sa, sb, hab⟩

/-
specMap respects identity.
-/
theorem specMap_id {S : Type u} [Semiring S] (x : ProofSpectrum S) :
    specMapSurj (RingHom.id S) surjective_id x = x := by
  ext a b; simp +decide [ specMapSurj ] ;
  exact Iff.rfl

/-
specMap respects composition.
-/
theorem specMap_comp {S T U : Type u} [Semiring S] [Semiring T] [Semiring U]
    (φ : S →+* T) (ψ : T →+* U)
    (hφ : Surjective φ) (hψ : Surjective ψ)
    (x : ProofSpectrum U) :
    specMapSurj φ hφ (specMapSurj ψ hψ x) =
    specMapSurj (ψ.comp φ) (hψ.comp hφ) x := by
  ext;
  exact Iff.rfl

/-
specMap is continuous.
-/
theorem specMapSurj_continuous {S T : Type u} [Semiring S] [Semiring T]
    (φ : S →+* T) (hφ : Surjective φ) :
    @Continuous (ProofSpectrum T) (ProofSpectrum S)
      (spectralTopology T) (spectralTopology S)
      (specMapSurj φ hφ) := by
  refine' continuous_generateFrom_iff.mpr _;
  rintro _ ⟨ a, b, rfl ⟩;
  convert basicOpenPair_isOpen ( φ a ) ( φ b ) using 1

/-
Preimage of a basic open under specMap is a basic open.
-/
theorem specMap_preimage_basicOpen {S T : Type u} [Semiring S] [Semiring T]
    (φ : S →+* T) (hφ : Surjective φ) (a b : S) :
    specMapSurj φ hφ ⁻¹' (basicOpenPair a b) = basicOpenPair (φ a) (φ b) := by
  grind

/-! ## §10: Finite Generation and Compactness -/

/-- A finitely generated proof semiring. -/
class FinitelyGeneratedProofSemiring (S : Type u) [Semiring S] : Prop where
  fg : ∃ (G : Finset S), ∀ a : S, a ∈ Subsemiring.closure (G : Set S)

/-
Compactness when the spectrum is finite.
-/
theorem spectrum_compact_of_finite {S : Type u} [Semiring S]
    [Finite (ProofSpectrum S)] :
    @CompactSpace (ProofSpectrum S) (spectralTopology S) :=
  Finite.compactSpace

/-! ## §11: Bridge to Ultrametric Dynamics -/

/-- A ProofStateContraction induces a DiagStableProofSystem. -/
def diagStableOfContraction {S : Type u}
    (C : ProofStateContraction S) : DiagStableProofSystem S where
  d := C.d
  isUltra := C.isUltra
  F := C.F
  diagonalStable := by
    intro x n
    have hcon := C.contractive
    have hq := C.hq_lt_one
    have hq0 := C.hq_nonneg
    have hnn := C.isUltra.1
    calc C.d (C.F^[n + 2] x) (C.F^[n + 1] x)
        = C.d (C.F (C.F^[n + 1] x)) (C.F (C.F^[n] x)) := by
          congr 1 <;> rw [Function.iterate_succ_apply']
      _ ≤ C.q * C.d (C.F^[n + 1] x) (C.F^[n] x) := hcon _ _
      _ ≤ 1 * C.d (C.F^[n + 1] x) (C.F^[n] x) := by
          apply mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_right hq.le (hnn _ _)
      _ = C.d (C.F^[n + 1] x) (C.F^[n] x) := one_mul _

/-
Iterate pair bound: geometric contraction.
-/
theorem iterate_pair_bound {S : Type u}
    (C : ProofStateContraction S) (x y : S) (n : ℕ) :
    C.d (C.F^[n] x) (C.F^[n] y) ≤ C.q ^ n * C.d x y := by
  induction' n with n ih;
  · simp +decide;
  · simpa only [ pow_succ', mul_assoc, Function.iterate_succ_apply' ] using le_trans ( C.contractive _ _ ) ( mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left ih C.hq_nonneg )

/-
Adjacent iterates decay geometrically.
-/
theorem iterate_step_bound {S : Type u}
    (C : ProofStateContraction S) (x : S) (n : ℕ) :
    C.d (C.F^[n+1] x) (C.F^[n] x) ≤ C.q ^ n * C.d (C.F x) x := by
  induction' n with n ih;
  · simp +decide;
  · simpa only [ pow_succ', mul_assoc, Function.iterate_succ_apply' ] using le_trans ( C.contractive _ _ ) ( mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left ih C.hq_nonneg )

/-! ## §12: Main Theorem Package -/

/-
**Proof Semiring Stone Duality Package**: CodeEq is a ring congruence,
